newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to rule on assisted-suicide ban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to rule on assisted-suicide ban.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday stepped into the right-to-die controversy by agreeing to decide whether mentally competent, terminally ill patients may seek help from their doctors in committing suicide.
The nation's highest court agreed to take up the emotional question of whether states may ban doctor-assisted suicide, an issue which has sparked a fierce national debate.

It will be one of the most important and closely watched issues the nine justices will decide during the 1996-97 term, which opens on Monday. The ruling could have broad impact as more than 30 states have made assisted suicide a crime.

Australia's Northern Territory legalised assisted suicide earlier this year, upholding the world's first voluntary euthanasia law. It allows terminally ill people to die by lethal injection or pills and went into force on July 1.
The U.S. high court's action to review laws from New York and Washington states banning physician-assisted suicide sets the stage for a possible landmark decision before July.

The justices in a pair of brief orders said they would hear appeals by New York and Washington of two precedent-setting rulings that struck down as unconstitutional laws that make it a crime for doctors to assist in a suicide.
The high court will hear oral arguments early next year.

The cases before the Supreme Court did not involve Dr. Jack Kevorkian, a retired pathologist and the nation's best known advocate of assisted suicide who has publicly acknowledged attending more than 40 deaths since 1990.
The right-to-die question presents the high court with one of the most wrenching and difficult dilemmas that it has to decide, rivaling the abortion rights dispute.

The Supreme Court last addressed the issue in 1990, ruling that a person has a constitutional right to refuse unwanted medical treatment in a case involving a comatose woman whose parents wanted to end artifical life support.

Supporters of doctor-assisted suicide argued it can spare a terminally ill patient needless pain and agony. But opponents, including the American Medical Association, replied it would be wrong for a physician to intentionally cause a patient's death.

President Bill Clinton has expressed his personal opposition to assisted suicide while Republican presidential rival Bob Dole criticised the two U.S. appeals court rulings that struck down the state laws.

One case reached the Supreme Court after an appeals court in March created a fundamental right to physician-assisted suicide. It cited the liberty protections of the due process clause in the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The San Fracisco-based appeals court ruled that mentally competent, terminally ill patients who wished to hasten their deaths to avoid protracted pain and suffering have a liberty interest in controlling the time and manners of their deaths.
Then, an appeals court in New York ruled in April that the prescription of drugs to hasten death was no different than the withdrawal of life support systems.

That ruling relied on the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. "Physicians who are willing to do so may prescribe drugs to be self-administered by mentally competent patients who seek to end their lives during the final stages of a terminal illness."

In appealing to the Supreme Court, New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco said, "The outcome of this case will have enormous influence on whether assisted suicide becomes a standard part of our nation's medical practice."
He said the case affected "what will occur in hospitals, clinics and doctors' offices around the country."

Washington Attorney General Christine Gregoire also appealed, saying the case presented an important issue of social policy. "A constitutional 'right to die' -- if it exists -- has implications for every American," she said.
